No rapport or lightness anywhere. Zero humor, zero personalization, no acknowledgment that moving into a bigger house (1,269 sqft to 2,300 sqft) is good news for this family.

No proactive FAQ handling and no budget-conscious framing. The customer twice signalled cost and time pressure (already packing, 'we work a lot') and was never told the one thing that was true and helpful — that the packing she has already done will shorten the job and lower her bill.

top_strength: This is a clean, disciplined intake and the routing decision was correct and well-reasoned. Jeline built a complete physical picture of both properties in under six minutes: she confirmed the origin address and zip, the 1,269 sqft two-story and its three bedrooms, then went hunting for volume the reps usually skip — 'are there any additional spaces where we have to get your things? Let's say do you have a garage, a backyard?' and then, crucially, 'is it a one car or a two car garage?' followed by 'is it completely full of your stuff or you can still park inside?' That second question is what separates a guess from an estimate, and she asked it unprompted. She cleared specialty items and appliances in sequence, caught the real inventory ('So, one fridge, one washer and two dryer' — read back to confirm), then repeated the whole geography exercise at the destination: address, zip, 2,300 sqft one-story, parking type at both ends, and access concerns with a specific prompt — 'like low hanging trees and client driveway or a few steps upstairs at the front door?' When the customer described a shared tight driveway and an inclined drop-off, Jeline pushed one level deeper on the contingency: 'but if ever ma'am, if we cannot do a driveway parking can we just park in front of your house?' Then she made the right call rather than the easy one. A partially self-packed home needing packing services is the single hardest thing to quote blind, and instead of guessing a number to get off the phone she said 'I really wanted to do a virtual walkthrough. So it's like a video call just for me to see all the things that we're gonna pack' — and closed it same-day, immediately, with 'would you like to do it right now?' Booking the walkthrough inside the same conversation, two to three minutes later, is the best possible version of that handoff.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: answer the question the customer actually asked. She told Jeline exactly what she wanted — 'I was just trying to see what a quote was cause we work a lot' — and the response was 'Understood. Okay, thank you.' That is the moment the call was won or lost, and it needed roughly this: 'LeeAnn, I hear you — you're both working and you don't have time for a runaround. Here's what I can tell you now: for a three-bedroom like yours we're usually looking at three movers and a truck, our rate is all-in with the gas, truck, wrap, pads and tools, and there's no deposit to hold your date. The reason I want a quick video walkthrough instead of guessing is that you've already packed part of the house, and I'd rather quote you on what's actually left than pad it — that usually saves people money. Two minutes on video and I'll have you a real number today.' Same routing decision, but now the customer knows why, knows roughly what she's dealing with, and knows the walkthrough is in her interest rather than another hoop. Second priority is the Save Your Ass speech, which was sitting right there. This customer said unprompted that she had already started packing and moving — she is self-selecting into the exact behavior the prep speech is designed to produce, and nobody told her it helps. She should have heard 'Everything you've already boxed up and carted over is money off your bill, so keep going if you can — the kids' toys, garden tools, anything loose in drawers, photos off the walls, and take a carload every time you drive over. The shorter our clock runs, the less you pay. Does that make sense?' That is a thirty-second add on a call that had room for it, and on a packing job it is the highest-dollar thirty seconds available. Third: use her name. It was verified in the first line and then replaced by 'ma'am' nine straight times, which reads deferential rather than warm. 'LeeAnn' three times across five minutes would have moved this call's whole temperature. Two things to fix in EMMA before the walkthrough: (1) the 50+ foot street carry at the origin and the shared tight driveway need to be logged as time variables — the customer stated both and neither was read back or confirmed as noted; (2) September 18 is a Friday twelve days out on a full-pack job and availability was never actually confirmed to her — verify the date is open and tell her so on the video call, because right now she believes she has a date and we have only acknowledged one.
phone_presence_notes: Courteous, patient and easy to follow — the customer answered every question cleanly and never asked her to repeat — but the language was formulaic to the point of repetition ('Okay, thank you' eight times, 'Mm-hmm' as a standalone reply to substantive answers), her name was swapped for 'ma'am' throughout, and the one emotional cue in the call ('we work a lot') drew a single flat 'Understood.'
audio_review_reason: Short call (5.7 min) with a near-monosyllabic customer ('Yeah.', 'Yes ma'am.', 'No.'), so there is thin signal on warmth either direction. Several rep lines are garbled in the transcript — 'do you have anything have you, like over to equipment a safe', 'anything valuable like our pieces or anti collection', and her own name rendered as 'juline' — and the clarity/pace bonus point was credited on the assumption those are ASR artifacts rather than real stumbles. Audio would confirm whether she was actually hard to follow, and whether the repeated 'Mm-hmm' landed as attentive or as dead air.
